The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC:      
Objective for processing: 
Project (1) Firstly to undertake regular work packages commissioned by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NIHCE), for which the University of Birmingham (UoB) are a designated Evidence Assessment Centre (EAC) until March 2017.  Typically these work packages are concerned with the adoption of novel treatments and devices in the NHS.  Often the UoB have to advise on the extent to which the diffusion of a novel treatment or device can (or cannot) be accurately mapped using routinely collected data. EAC packages arise at short notice with no prior communication of the subject area. One recurring area of work is to comment on the suitability of HES as a means of surveillance of the diffusion of evolving technologies.  Current examples of work packages are: the use of ultra-radical surgery in the treatment of ovarian cancer, the use of selective internal radiotherapy treatment in patients with metastatic cancer and the use of extra-corporal carbon dioxide removal in the intensive care of trauma patients. These projects will, by the nature of the specific work package requested, utilise various elements of the HES dataset.  The examples include various sections of the dataset which include procedural, diagnostic, admission, discharge and spell fields which is why the entire dataset is required.  Only the data which is necessary for that work package will be analysed and reported upon. 
A specific example where the whole dataset is required  is: “NICE’s Interventional Procedures Programme may issue guidance to the NHS that certain procedures may only be used if patients are entered onto a register to collect further evidence on safety and efficacy. One example is extra-corporeal carbon dioxide removal (ECCOR) a life-support intervention for critically ill patients. This uses specialist equipment to remove carbon dioxide from blood as opposed to oxygenating it. Some small scale studies have suggested there could be a large decrease in mortality associated with the technique. In the absence of a large scale study, no specific NICE guidelines exist as to the use of the technique in England. We are using HES to scope current use and help to plan a registry to support the collection of outcomes data. We will capture case volumes and sites, together with case-mix variables.  We use this to determine where ECCOR is used and how often by running queries quarterly which capture case counts by hospital with demographic and diagnostic indicators and outcomes (discharged alive / died). 
This will be used to assess data capture completeness in a national registry, and tell us if and when new ECCOR users arise so they can be invited to support the registry.   If the data in the registry support the findings of smaller studies, and widespread introduction is recommended this would contribute to an increase in survival in the treatment of critically ill patients.  If we conclude there is no evidence to support introduction, because of no credible survival gain, hospitals would avoid buying the (very expensive) equipment and save money.”
In this example the entire dataset will enable cross comparative analysis to be carried to quantify cases where ECCOR has been used (using specific OPCS 4.6 codes) against total number of inpatient episodes by hospital provider. 
 
Project (2) Secondly to deliver a programme of applied health services research under the Collaboration for Leadership in Applied Health Research and Care programme (CLAHRC). This is an NIHR funded programme in which the leading academic health care institutions in the UK work with the NHS and other providers of health and social care in a three year programme of with multiple themed research streams. In the case of the West Midlands CLAHRC, this answering research questions about patient flows through secondary care systems and the resulting outcomes in the West Midlands population.  To do this the University of Birmingham need contextual data on the English acute hospital population to make valid comparisons, using metrics such as length of stay, in-hospital mortality rates and readmission applied to various groups of patients, determined by epidemiology, demography or service use derived from HES data.  Much of the work undertaken is traditional academic research, principally cross-sectional observational studies resulting in peer reviewed publications. However the University of Birmingham will also be undertaking 'action research' and service evaluation in response to changes in service configuration service configuration. This activity will generate outputs whose main aim is to communicate assessments of service quality safety and cost-effectiveness to stakeholders, such as monograph reports and other forms of 'grey' literature. There is a deliberate degree of permeability in the University of Birmingham’s NIHR work programmes between research and service evaluation in accordance with the wishes of the commissioner and the guiding philosophy of CLAHRC.  This project is funded until 31st December 2019.

Project (3)  Thirdly the University of Birmingham are running an NIHR funded project, the High Level Specialist Led Acute Care project (ethics reference number 13/WA/0372) to determine the impact of different models of consultant working at weekends on the excess mortality in acute hospitals that occurs in patients admitted during these times. This project will run from 2014 with a proposed conclusion date of 31st January 2019. It will evaluate the roll out of the Government’s seven day services initiative. It will include an analysis of -trends in hospital mortality from 2007-2008 (by mortality it is meant as measured by the ‘dismeth’ variable and not related to ONS mortality data) onwards, will examine the association between a measure of specialist intensity captured in approximately 120 acute trusts in England, and in-hospital mortality in financial year 2013/14 to provide a baseline analysis.  The University of Birmingham will go on to repeat the analysis until the end of the project to measure how this association changes over time as the Seven Day Services implementation extends throughout the service.
None of these above activities are commercial.  None involve for-profit work, commercialisation of research outputs or the development of intellectual property. 
Record level data will not be shared with any third party and only used by the University of Birmingham.  No commercial organisation is involved in any of this work.

Processing activities: 
For (1) above:
•           Use the HES Inpatient, Outpatient and A&E data to aggregate summary data to report on trends in the use of specific treatments as specified by NICE EAC work packages.
•           This includes numbers population rates and capture of other variables where appropriate such as length of stay, discharge method, neighbourhood deprivation scores and re-admission rates.
•           Depending on the work package; this will include the processing of 1 or more years of HES data . 
 
For (2) above: 
•           Use the HES Inpatient, Outpatient and A&E data to  derive directly standardised rates of admissions in various diagnostic groups defined by HRGs, main diagnostic profiles or surgical procedures.  
•           Use the HES Inpatient, Outpatient and A&E data to analyse individual level data and produce aggregated outputs for the construction of statistical models to test specific hypotheses about the association between changes to service configuration in uses.
•           Capturing outcomes data for a longitudinal observational study into the outcomes associated with early discharge following childbirth in England.
•           This project will utilise multiple years of HES Inpatient, Outpatient and A&E data 
For (3) above: 
•           A multi-level model of hospital mortality and its association with a range of variables captured in the HES Inpatient, Outpatient and A&E datasets and a measure of specialist intensity captured by a point prevalence survey in a sample of approximately 120 hospitals. For context the University of Birmingham will also be building a more general model of mortality based on the HES data in this application.  This will require historical data going back to financial year 2007/08 

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
For (1) above:
•           A report on the feasibility of using routinely collected data to map the use and outcomes of selective internal radiotherapy treatment.
•           A report on the feasibility of using routinely collected data to monitor the use of ultra-radical surgery in the treatment of ovarian cancer.
For (2) above:
•           A report on urgent care provision in Worcestershire.  Specifically comparing the relationship between urgent care access and socio-economic status (as measured by neighbourhood income deprivation) and comparing this to statistical neighbours for the County’s population.  The University of Birmingham plan to produce a written report for local stakeholders in December 2015.

•           An evaluation of how three natural experiments arising from three changes in service configuration change affect demand for Emergency Department (ED) attendance namely an ED closure, an ED relocation and the opening of a Minor Injury Unit.  This builds on existing work carried out in the Department which has been published in peer-reviewed scientific literature by the applicant.  We plan to submit these studies to peer-reviewed journals by mid-year 2016.

•           A report on bariatric surgery uptake in the Region compared to the rest of England.  Specifically modelling uptake and assessing the differential association between estimates population obesity, socio-economic status, proximity to provider and demographic factors. Submitted for peer reviewed publication mid-year 2016

•           A study of patient pathways for paediatric allergy services, including a systematic review, and assessment of current use of and demand for allergy services and a health economic assessment of different models of service delivery.  This will include assessment of demand, temporal trends and current patterns of service contact using HES. This will include of design of a West Midlands service pathway.  Outputs will include peer review publication and reports and feedback to regional and national stakeholders between the present and 31st December 2018.

•           A study of the Frequency of obesity as a diagnostic code in paediatric admissions in the West Midlands.

•           A longitudinal observational study into the outcomes associated with early discharge following childbirth in England, completion by 31st January 2019.  Report to funders and submission of a paper in the peer reviewed academic literature. 
For (3) above: 

•           A statistical model estimating the correlation between a measure of intensity of specialist care cove and case-mix adjusted mortality rates in English Hospitals for financial 2013/14. Target date:  ASAP 
•           Temporal trends in English hospital mortality from 2003 to 2016. Target date: June 2017. 
•           A paper in the peer reviewed scientific literature on the association between specialist led care intensity and hospital mortality.  Target submission date: calendar year end 2015.
•           An interim report to the project steering committee and then for wider stakeholder distribution at calendar year end 2017, including an assessment of changes in hospital mortality between 2013/14 – 2016/17.
•           A full report to the project steering committee and then for wider stakeholder distribution will be completed by 31st January 2019 with quarterly reports until the project end.
•           A paper in the peer reviewed scientific literature on the association between specialist led care intensity and hospital mortality, including ethnographic research and analysis of case note reviews is expected to be submitted towards the end of calendar year 2018.
•           A paper proposing and validating a new hospital taxonomy for the English NHS, using a novel case-mix measurement method has been conceived and will be submitted for publication within 6 months of a 2013/14 data set being available for analysis.  
•           Econometric modelling will also be done to evaluate the extent to which changes in policy result in cost savings as well as patient outcomes. Results of this will be included in the final report. It is likely that they will be separately submitted to a peer-reviewed scientific journal at or around the project end date. 

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
Please note that for all three uses of the data, the funder is an NHS organisation, and thus would argue that there is a benefit for this work within the health and social care sector.
For (1) above: 
•           To assist in the formulation of national best practice guidelines for emerging medical technologies.
•           To determine where routine data collection can be used instead of specialist registries in the capture of outcomes data for guideline development.  Where this is the case, time and money can be saved.  
For (2) above
•           Service stakeholders to obtain decision support data to improve patient pathways and outcomes across a number of different services, from small changes to reduce delays and improve access to appropriate care, up to and including complete service re-design between now and the project end date of 31st December 2019.
•           It is recognised that paediatric service pathways in allergy services are not optimal in the University of Birmingham’s region, and that recommended pathway designs call for consultant expertise that is not available.  Development of feasible pathways for the West midlands informed by an assessment of current demand and needs should result improved access to evidence based diagnosis and treatment of allergy in paediatric patients.
•           Further information on the contribution of obesity to paediatric hospital admissions will quantify the need for hospital-based interventions targeting obesity in children and young people and will contribute to service design.
•           Knowledge transfer is a critical part of the CLAHRC philosophy in which capacity in analysis of clinical data is enhanced by service partners, across all areas of the collaboration.
For (3) above: 
•           To inform national policy on the implementation of 24/7 consultant working in England.
•           Improved patient outcomes, possibly with cost savings would be expected as a result of this important policy change, however the University of Birmingham need high quality data driven research and analysis to confirm this. These would be elucidated in the final report of the project produced in 2019.
